Also the original site of the runestone Kuregaardsstenen (moved in 1857 to Klemens Churchyard). Listed as entry 72 in F.O. Nielsen (1997, p. 3).

notes: Major Late Germanic Iron Age and Viking Age cemetery (c. 520/530–850 AD) located on a sand-covered beach ridge (strandvold) on Lousgård's coastal plot (Østerlars Sb. 114 / Sb. 143 / loknr 114 / stednr 60405 / systemnr 123466 / frednr 5135103 / anlnr 06.04.05; Matr. Nr. 20 b). Excavated in 1886–1887 and 1902 by E. Vedel and J.A. Jørgensen (52 inhumations, 1 cremation). Re-analyzed by H. Lyngstrøm (1989) and L. Jørgensen (2010). Features horizontal stratigraphy of a single elite family lineage buried over 6.75 generations (~270 years) under/in stone pavements/cairns (røser) up to 9.5 m in diameter. Seriation by K. Høilund Nielsen (1987) identifies Phase 1A-B (6 female inhumations, 530–600 AD), Phase 1C-D (2 female inhumations, 600–680/700 AD), Phase 2A-C (5 female inhumations, 680/700–775/800 AD), and Early Viking Age (4 female inhumations, 800–850 AD). Includes 15 male weapon burials (single-edged seaxes, lances, shield bosses) dating to 500–600s AD; weapon deposition ceases in the 700s AD across Bornholm due to strict inheritance laws. Famous burials include Grav 47 (richest female grave under 9.5 m cairn with gilt garnet brooch, 55 beads, and sacrificed servant/horse 32 cm above) and Grav 48 (male grave with horse/servant sacrifice). Listed as entry 261 in F.O. Nielsen (1997, p. 3) and published in Vedel (1897, pp. 143ff).

notes: Situated on coastal beach ridge (matr.nr. 123c & 123d) south of Gudhjem, Melsted (Sandhuset) is a  coastal cemetery spanning the Migration Period, Late Germanic Iron Age, and Viking Age (c. 400–900 AD). Originally featured around 40 small mounds and cairns registered in 1870. Systematically excavated in 1877 and 1880 by E. Vedel and J.A. Jørgensen, recording 18  numbered burials under stone pavements and cairns. Inhumation burials dominate. Rich weapon graves include double-edged swords, seaxes, lance heads, shield bosses, and Grave 1 which contained a unique blacksmith's tool chest (hammer, anvil, tongs). Rich female burials feature gilded relief brooches, tortoise brooches, and glass beads.

notes: Situated on a sand ridge near the dune belt northwest of Due Odde at Store Munkegård (28. & 29. Sg., historically also known as Pæregaard) in Poulsker parish, Munkegaard is a major multi-period cemetery spanning the Iron Age through the Early Middle Ages/Viking Age (c. 500 BC – 1100 AD). Excluding earlier Bronze Age mound features, the site's Iron Age and early Christian excavation history is documented across several campaigns: 1) 1878 (Nationalmuseet): Excavated 25–30 Viking Age/early medieval W–E inhumations containing iron coffin nails and utility knives, dug directly into an Early Roman Iron Age cremation field where ~14 cremation pits (brandpletter) were examined (yielding a crescent-shaped razor). 2) 1928–1933 / 1943 (E. Albrectsen, Journal 109/46): Road construction along Strandmarksvejen unearthed 25–30 additional skeletons and cremation pits, alongside previously plowed-up urns and a Roman coin. 3) 1997 (Bornholms Museum, BMR 1071, H. Wagnkilde & H. Høier): Investigated 3,800 m², locating 150 W–E row-graves (35 excavated) in plank coffins with iron rivets and trough-shaped log coffins from the 1000s AD. Finds (knives, beads, coins, pottery) proved strict spatial gender division: women in the preserved northern section, men in the destroyed southern section. Also examined 11 of 32 Early Roman cremation pits. 4) 1999 (BMR 1071): Excavated >700 m² east/west of the main field. West field revealed 36 Pre-Roman/Early Roman cremation pits (10 excavated with belt hooks, iron fibulae, and a gold-foil bead). East field revealed 8 cremation pits and 17 late Viking/early medieval graves, where 5 Svend Estridsen silver coins (1047–1074 AD) dated the Christian cemetery precisely. Traces of an eastern Iron Age settlement were also noted. 5) 2002 & 2018 (Bornholms Museum & Nationalmuseet Ødekirker Project, N. Engberg): Confirmed ~170 preserved row-graves in the northern female section (with ~105 inhumations and ~44 cremation pits remaining unexcavated in the core area), while the male southern section was lost to roadwork. A related sub-location, Munkegård ØSØ, is registered separately as systemnr 195261 (Poulsker Sb. 93). Catalogued as entry 178 in F.O. Nielsen (1997, p. 6) and Poulsker Sb. 24.

Monuments_notes: Located on rocky knolls (klippeknuder) near the old mill. Originally comprised ~10 low earthen mounds/barrows (jordkuller/høje), stone settings (stensætninger), and cremation pit fields (brandpletter). Two mounds were exceptionally broad (~160 feet / 50 m diameter) but low (1.5–3 feet high).
source: Fund og Fortidsminder (systemnr 1968, Østerlars Sb. 89 / Gudhjem Sb. 180); Vedel, E. (1886, s. 372; 1897, s. 125); Engelhardt, C. (1868, s. 135f); Nationalmuseet (1866, 1880, 1948, Journal 681/48).
notes: Situated on rocky knolls (klippeknuder) near the old mill southwest of Gudhjem in Østerlars parish (Østerlars Sb. 89 / Gudhjem Sb. 180), Møllebakken is a major multi-phased Iron Age cemetery (c. 1–749 AD). Features include Early Roman cremation pits (1–374 AD) and Germanic Iron Age barrows, stone settings, and cremation pits (375–749 AD). Site history: 1) 1866: Workers digging in an earthen mound uncovered Iron Age artifacts in April. In July 1866, Prof. C. Engelhardt excavated the two largest low mounds (~160 feet / 50 m in diameter, 1.5–3 feet high), revealing extraordinarily rich female burials (published in Aarbøger 1868, pp. 135–136; Vedel 1886, p. 372). 2) 1880: Nationalmuseet survey recorded ~10 mounds on the rocky knolls. Former landowner H.A. West donated gold and silver items found in a small mound near the old mill: a cut spiral gold wire ring (3/8 lod / ~4.8g) and 3 gilded silver fibulae, 2 curved fittings, and 3 embossed silver/gold beads (7 3/16 lod / ~113g). 3) 1948 (Nationalmuseet Journal 681/48): Excavation of a cremation pit near the mounds.

notes: Situated on a sandy rise known as Møllehøjen north of Vedbygård (Skovvang) in Olsker parish (Olsker Sb. 53 / systemnr 122429 / loknr 53 / stednr 60105 / anlnr 06.01.05), Møllehøj is an Early Roman Iron Age cremation pit cemetery (c. 175–374 AD). Investigations by C.J. Becker in 1943–1944 (Nationalmuseet J.nr. 363/50) excavated 6 cremation pit graves (Graves 9–14 / NM C 24753–24782), recovering iron utility knives, an iron rim fitting, a spindle whorl (tenvægt), double-conical vessels, pitchers, and beakers. Deep plowing in the winter of 1998–1999 exposed dark soil discolorations of an additional 30–35 heavily damaged cremation pit graves, which were inspected and recorded by Bornholms Museum (BMR 2645). Catalogued as entry 21 in F.O. Nielsen (1997, p. 1) and published in Vedel (1886, s. 306).

Munch and Nationalmuseet recorded inhumation graves yielding single-edged swords (seaxes), lance heads, shield bosses, bronze fibulae, glass beads, and pottery. 2) 1954 (Nationalmuseet Journal 633/54): Site grading during construction work uncovered 4 ceramic vessels from 2 Late Roman cremation graves (brandgrave, c. 175–374 AD), submitted to Bornholms Museum. status: Recorded Late Roman Iron Age strandgrave / cemetery site in Nexø parish.
notes: Situated on the coastal shingle beach (Strandmarken) north of Nexø town near the abandoned Frederiks Sandstone Quarry (Frederiks Stenbrud) in Nexø parish (Nexø Sb. 7 / systemnr 122621 / loknr 7 / stednr 60202 / anlnr 06.02.02), this site is a Late Roman Iron Age cemetery of beach graves (strandgrave / voldgrave, c. 175–375 AD). Excavated in 1880 by Emil Vedel and J.A. Jørgensen, over 25 graves under stone mounds/depressions along ancient beach ridges were investigated. Recorded finds from individual graves include bronze fibulae (Type F2, ligearmede fibuler), iron dress pins, sword fragments (voldgrav 21), a bronze pincet/niptang in a stone cist with burnt bones (BO s. 298 Nr. 18), and a bead necklace with 160 glass and amber beads (voldgrav 12). Catalogued as entry 199 in F.O. Nielsen (1997, p. 5) and published in Vedel (1886, s. 363–365; 1897, s. 124, 128).

Monuments_notes: Cemetery field under stone heaps and pavements (stendynger, brolægninger) on farmland (Matr. 11a, 123h) extending towards Kobbe Å.
Weapons_notes: Contains weapon burials, most notably Kobbe Å Grav 36 (NM C 6178–81, re-assigned to Nørre Sandegård), which contained a spatha (double-edged sword), a seax (single-edged sword, Type V1A), a shield boss, knife, and pot. Also includes cremation pits with belt hooks/fibulae and rich female graves.
source: Fund og Fortidsminder (systemnr 2014, Østerlars Sb. 154 / Sb. 108); Vedel, E. (1886, s. 376; 1897, s. 143); Becker, C.J. (1948–1952, NM Ark.afd. 1805–1819); Nielsen, F.O. (1997, p. 8, entry 256).
status: Recorded cremation and inhumation cemetery in Østerlars parish.
notes: Situated ~1 km south of Melsted on farmland belonging to Nørre Sandegård (Matr. 11a, 123h) in Østerlars parish (Østerlars Sb. 154 / Sb. 108 / systemnr 2014 / loknr 154 / stednr 60405 / anlnr 06.04.05; Ark.afd. 1805–1819), Nr. Sandegaard is a multi-phased Iron Age cemetery (c. 500 BC – 800 AD) closely connected with the adjacent Kobbe Å site (Sb. 108). Excavations by E. Vedel and J.A. Jørgensen (1884, 1887–1888, 1901) and C.J. Becker (1948–1952) uncovered Pre-Roman and Early Roman cremation pit graves (brandpletter) as well as Late Roman and Germanic Iron Age inhumations under stone heaps. Finds include beaked brooches, button brooches, shears, knives, spindle whorls, and bead sets. Catalogued as entry 256 (alongside Sb. 108) in F.O. Nielsen (1997, p. 8).

Monuments_notes: Cemetery field near Ny Mølle recorded as 3 cremation pits (brandpletgrave) in Fund og Fortidsminder, though 1876 Nationalmuseet investigation notes suggest inhumation burials in dark soil stains (ubrændt grav).
Weapons_notes: Contains an elite blacksmith/warrior burial (Grav 1) with an iron lance head (12 inch long, 3 inch wide), shield boss, lance butt shoe (dupsko), blacksmithing hammer, anvil (2.5 inch high, 1.5 inch wide), smithing tongs (11 inch long), chest fittings with brass rivets, whetstone, and red beads.
source: Fund og Fortidsminder (systemnr 647, Nexø Sb. 1, 1876 berejsning); Vedel, E. (1886, s. 365; 1897, s. 129); Nationalmuseet (1873 Journal, NM C 1685–1699).
status: Recorded Iron Age inhumation cemetery and blacksmith grave site in Nexø parish.
notes: Located at Ny Mølle (Nymølle) just west/northwest of Nexø town north of the Rønne-Nexø road in Nexø parish (Nexø Sb. 1 / systemnr 647 / loknr 1 / stednr 60202 / anlnr 06.02.02), this site is an Iron Age cemetery field (c. 175–800 AD). Discovered in 1873 during site clearance for a new building by the miller, 3 dark soil pits with unburnt human bones were uncovered. 1876 Nationalmuseet investigation notes suggest inhumation burials in dark soil stains (ubrændt grav), though Fund og Fortidsminder lists 3 cremation pits. Grave 1 (NM C 1685–1695) is a famous elite blacksmith/warrior burial in a chest with iron fittings and brass rivets, containing a hammer, anvil (2.5 inch high, 1.5 inch wide), smithing tongs (11 inch long), shield boss, broad lance head (12 inch long, 3 inch wide), lance butt shoe (dupsko), gilded bronze studs, whetstone, knife, and red beads. Grave 2 (NM C 1696–1698) contained a bronze spiral, knife, and 61 beads (11 white, 8 green, 41 red, 1 yellow). Grave 3 yielded a broad lance head and a knife. Published in Vedel (1886, s. 365; 1897, s. 129).

Monuments_notes: Inhumation chamber graves, plank coffins, boat graves, ring ditches (ringgrøfter), and low cairns/mounds (røser) on a moraine hill terrace ~200–300 m inland from the coast.
Weapons_notes: Lavish warrior burials containing single-edged and double-edged swords (spatha, sax), shield bosses with tinned bronze studs, lance heads, axes, horse harnessry with tinned rivets, and horse burials (e.g. Graves 1, 3, 5, 21, 24, 27, 29, 30, 31, 35, 36, 42, 60).
source: Fund og Fortidsminder (systemnr 123498, Østerlars Sb. 183); Vedel, E. (1886, 1897); Jørgensen, L. & Nørgård Jørgensen, A. (1997); Bornholms Museum (BMR 1409, 1986–1987, 2013–2016); Nielsen, F.O. (1997, p. 8, entry 257).
status: Systematically excavated Late Germanic Iron Age cemetery in Østerlars parish.
notes: Located ~1 km south of Melsted and ~200–300 m inland from the coast at Nørre Sandegård in Østerlars parish (Østerlars Sb. 183 / systemnr 123498 / loknr 183 / stednr 60405 / anlnr 06.04.05; BMR 1409), Nørre Sandegård Vest is one of Scandinavia's premier Late Germanic Iron Age / Merovingian cemeteries (c. 520–800 AD), with underlying Roman Iron Age cremation activity (c. 175–375 AD). Initially recognized by Emil Vedel (1884–1901, 7 graves including Kobbe Å 33), extensive rescue excavations by Lars Jørgensen and B.B. Hansen (Bornholms Museum, BMR 1409, 1986–1987) uncovered 47 Merovingian inhumations and 26 Roman cremation pits across >3,000 m². Subsequent excavations in 2013–2016 added 26 inhumations and 4 chamber graves. The site is famous for rich chamber graves, horse burials, boat graves, warrior weapon sets, and elite female ornament graves with tortoise brooches, relief brooches, glass/amber bead sets, and textile remains. Catalogued as entry 257 in F.O. Nielsen (1997, p. 8) and fully published in Jørgensen & Nørgård Jørgensen (1997).

Monuments_notes: Secondary inhumation burial and 2 urn burials set into an older Bronze Age barrow/mound (ældre høj) on farmland belonging to Nørregaard in Østerlars parish.
Weapons_notes: Contains a rich warrior burial (NM C 2747–58) with an iron lance head (lansespids), bridle with 2 square strap-divider fittings (bidsel med 2 kvadratiske remfordelerbeslag), strap end (remendedup), horse harness fittings, knife, and horse bones/skull (hestehoved).
source: Fund og Fortidsminder (systemnr 1989, Østerlars Sb. 105 / Sb. 104); Vedel, E. (1886, s. 374); Jørgensen, L. (1989).
status: Recorded Late Germanic Iron Age barrow burial site in Østerlars parish.
notes: Located at Nørregaard (Nørregård) in Østerlars parish (Østerlars Sb. 105 / Sb. 104 / systemnr 1989 / loknr 105 / stednr 60405 / anlnr 06.04.05), this site features a secondary Late Germanic Iron Age warrior inhumation burial (c. 550–750 AD) inserted into an older Bronze Age barrow, opened in 1877. The burial inventory (NM C 2747–2758) includes a lance head, knife, horse bridle bits with square strap-divider mounts, strap ends, and horse skull remains (hestehoved). At least two urn burials from the Late Germanic Iron Age were also uncovered in the same mound. Published in Vedel (1886, s. 374) and catalogued by L. Jørgensen (1989).

Monuments_notes: Secondary Iron Age cremation graves and Viking Age equestrian inhumation (ryttergrav) set into the top of a large Bronze Age barrow (~100 ft diameter).
Weapons_notes: Contains a Viking Age equestrian warrior grave (ryttergrav) with a 9.5-inch iron lance head (NM C 2747–2758), knife, bridle bits, bronze harness fittings, square horse harness ornament, horse jaw/teeth, and 6 red beads. status: Recorded Iron Age cremation and Viking Age equestrian barrow burial site in Østerlars parish.
notes: Located at Nørregaard (Nørregård) in Østerlars parish (Østerlars Sb. 104 / systemnr 1988 / loknr 104 / stednr 60405 / anlnr 06.04.05), this site is a large overploughed Bronze Age barrow (~100 ft diameter) containing secondary Iron Age burials. In spring 1877, a stone-lined equestrian warrior inhumation (ryttergrav, 1 Alen deep) was uncovered at the top of the mound, yielding a 9.5-inch iron lance head, knife, bridle bits with bronze harness fittings, a square bronze horse head mount, horse jaw fragments, and 6 red beads. Nearby (6-8 Alen east), 2 cremation pit/pot burials filled with burnt bones (dated 1–374 AD) were found. In 1996, Bronze Age sword fragments (BMR 2451 / NM B 17769-70) were detector-found on the overploughed mound.
